SubTopics: Students will determine the key details that support the main idea of a text.
Content: Which sentence from the passage `ultext(best)` supports the idea that sleep is important to learning?

A.Choice: Scientists have been trying to answer that question for `text(hundreds of years)`.

Key.Rationale: This sentence is too vague to support the idea that sleep is important to learning.

B.Choice: The dreams give us a safe way to handle the events of our day.

Key.Rationale: This sentence does not address the idea that sleep is important to learning, but addresses how dreams help us to cope with events of our day.

C.Choice: Scientists think that their brains were trying to quickly memorize and organize this new information.

Key.Rationale: This sentence supports the idea that sleep is important to learning by discussing how our brains are able to memorize and organize new information.

D.Choice: She asked her students to think about a problem they had before going to sleep.

Key.Rationale: This sentence does not support the idea that sleep is important to learning.

SubTopics: Students will compare fiction, poetry, and nonfiction to distinguish various genres.
Content: A reader can tell that this passage is nonfiction because it

A.Choice: explains something with factual information.

Key.Rationale: This passage relates factual information, a prominent feature of nonfiction text, about why we dream.

B.Choice: is written with very short sentences.

Key.Rationale: The length of the sentences is unrelated to whether or not the passage is nonfiction.

C.Choice: has words spoken by a character.

Key.Rationale: Nonfiction passages generally do not have characters. Characters are common feature of fiction.

D.Choice: is divided into several sections.

Key.Rationale: Both fiction and nonfiction passages can be divided into several sections, so this is not a discerning feature.

SubTopics: Students will find textual evidence of literary devices.
Content: Which sentence from “Why Do We Dream?” contains a simile?

A.Choice: You are flying through the clouds.

Key.Rationale: A simile is a comparison between `text(two)` things. Nothing is being compared in this sentence.

B.Choice: Down below, the earth looks like a patchwork quilt.

Key.Rationale: The way the earth looks from a cloud is being compared to a patchwork quilt.

C.Choice: The beautiful bird reaches out and shakes your arm.

Key.Rationale: A simile is a comparison between `text(two)` things. Nothing is being compared in this sentence.

D.Choice: You are back in your own bedroom.

Key.Rationale: A simile is a comparison between `text(two)` things. Nothing is being compared in this sentence.

SubTopics: Students will distinguish fact from opinion in an informational text and explain how reasons and facts support specific points.
Content: Which statement in the article is an `ultext(opinion)`?

A.Choice: Scientists have been trying to answer that question for `text(hundreds of years)`.

Key.Rationale: This is a fact which can be measured.

B.Choice: `text(One)` study showed that people learning new activities dreamed much more often.

Key.Rationale: This is a fact that can be verified by the scientific study.

C.Choice: `text(Two-thirds)` of the students dreamed about their problems.

Key.Rationale: This is a fact that can be verified by Barrett's study.

D.Choice: That must have been one scary nightmare!

Key.Rationale: This is an opinion about the Frankenstein inspiration Mary Shelley had from a dream.

SubTopics: Students will use context clues to clarify the meaning of words.
Content: In paragraph `2`, the word `ultext(theories)` means

A.Choice: ideas.

Key.Rationale: “Ideas” is correct because the word “theories” means systems of ideas intended to explain something.

B.Choice: plans.

Key.Rationale: The word “theories” means systems of ideas intended to explain something, not plans.

C.Choice: pictures.

Key.Rationale: The word “theories” means systems of ideas intended to explain something, not pictures.

D.Choice: questions.

Key.Rationale: The word “theories” means systems of ideas intended to explain something, not questions.

SubTopics: Students will identify relationships among words, including synonyms, antonyms, analogies, homophones, and homographs.
Content: An antonym for `ultext(remember)` in paragraph `7` is

A.Choice: enjoy.

Key.Rationale: This is not the antonym for “remember” which means to recall.

B.Choice: forget.

Key.Rationale: This is the opposite for the word “remember” which means to recall.

C.Choice: create.

Key.Rationale: This is not the antonym for “remember” which means to recall.

D.Choice: describe.

Key.Rationale: This is not the antonym for “remember” which means to recall.

SubTopics: Students will identify and use text features (e.g., graphics, captions, headings/subheadings, bold/italicized words, charts, tables, legends) to comprehend informational texts.
Content: Why are the section headings in bold print?

A.Choice: to help the reader with new information

Key.Rationale: The section headings in bold print will not help the reader with new information presented.

B.Choice: to help the reader find important information quickly

Key.Rationale: By looking at the topics of the section headings in bold print, the reader can locate particular information.

C.Choice: to help the reader understand the information better

Key.Rationale: The section headings in bold print will not help the reader with understanding the new information presented.

D.Choice: to help the reader remember the most important information

Key.Rationale: The section headings in bold print will not help the reader to remember the new information presented.

SubTopics: Students will summarize facts and details from an informational text.
Content: Which sentence `ultext(best)` summarizes paragraph `4` of “The American Buffalo”?

A.Choice: Settlers sold buffalo hides for money.

Key.Rationale: This is just `text(one)` detail presented in paragraph `4`.

B.Choice: Settlers hunted the buffalo for entertainment.

Key.Rationale: This is just `text(one)` detail presented in paragraph `4`.

C.Choice: Settlers did not know how many buffalo there were, and they almost hunted the buffalo out of existence.

Key.Rationale: This is not a detail presented in paragraph `4`.

D.Choice: Settlers did not value the buffalo in the same way others did, which almost caused the buffalo to die out.

Key.Rationale: This sentence summarizes the main ideas presented in paragraph `4`.

SubTopics: Students will compare fiction, poetry, and nonfiction to distinguish various genres.
Content: Select `bbtext(two)` statements to show the features of informational text and poetry.

SubTopics: Students will determine the key details that support the main idea of a text.
Content: Which sentence from “The American Buffalo” supports the statement “These settlers did not have the same respect for the buffalo as the Native Americans”?

A.Choice: They want to protect them.

Key.Rationale: Wanting to protect the buffalo does not support the idea of not having the same respect for the buffalo.

B.Choice: This herd is carefully protected.

Key.Rationale: Carefully protecting the herd does not support the idea of not having the same respect for the buffalo.

C.Choice: Many of the settlers were trappers and traders.

Key.Rationale: The fact that many settlers were trappers and traders does not directly support the idea of not having the same respect for the buffalo.

D.Choice: These settlers killed more than what they needed.

Key.Rationale: The idea of the settlers killing more buffalo that what was needed does support the idea of not having the same respect for the buffalo.

SubTopics: Students will organize information found during research, following a modified citation style (i.e., author, title, publication year).
Content: The information in a citation follows this order: author, title, year of publication.
Show the correct order of the citation.

SubTopics: Students will determine the author’s purpose (i.e., entertain, inform, persuade) by identifying key details.
Content: The author of “The American Buffalo” `ultext(most likely)` wrote this passage

A.Choice: to inform the reader with details.

Key.Rationale: This passage presents historical and modern day information about the American buffalo to the reader.

B.Choice: to persuade the reader with facts.

Key.Rationale: This passage presents historical and modern day facts about the American buffalo and is not trying to persuade the reader.

C.Choice: to entertain the reader with a story.

Key.Rationale: This passage presents historical and modern day facts about the American buffalo and is not entertaining the reader with a story.

D.Choice: to share a personal experience with the reader.

Key.Rationale: This passage presents historical and modern day facts about the American buffalo and is not sharing a personal experience with the reader.

SubTopics: Students will determine whether a grade-level literary text is narrated in first- or third-person point of view.
Content: “The American Buffalo” is told from which point of view?

A.Choice: first person by someone who works to help buffalo

Key.Rationale: The passage is not written in the first person.

B.Choice: first person by someone who hunts buffalo

Key.Rationale: The passage is not written in the first person.

C.Choice: third person by an unknown narrator

Key.Rationale: The passage is written by an unknown narrator relating information as an outsider looking in and using the pronoun “they.”

D.Choice: third person by an unknown settler

Key.Rationale: The passage is not written in the third person by an unknown settler.

SubTopics: Students will distinguish the structures of an informational text.
Content: Describe how the author structures paragraphs `4` and `5` of “The American Buffalo.” Provide details from the passage to support your answer.

SubTopics: Students will answer inferential questions using evidence from one or more texts to support answers.
Content: Why did the attitudes about buffalo change?

A.Choice: People realized that buffalo were going to disappear.

Key.Rationale: Once people realized that the American buffalo was becoming extinct, they began efforts that would preserve and protect the buffalo.

B.Choice: People realized that buffalo were becoming too small.

Key.Rationale: The weight of the buffalo has decreased from long ago, but the passage does not support the idea that that is why people changed their attitude about buffalo.

C.Choice: People realized that others depended on buffalo for survival.

Key.Rationale: Although the passage indicates that Native Americans and early settlers depended on the buffalo for survival, the passage does not suggest that people continue to depend on buffalo for survival.

D.Choice: People realized that buffalo were not crossing the land bridge anymore.

Key.Rationale: The land bridge no longer connects North America and Asia.

SubTopics: Students will conduct research to answer questions, including self-generated questions, and to build knowledge, using multiple sources (e.g., visual and text reference sources, electronic resources, and/or interviews).
Content: Which question would be `ultext(best)` to use to find information about preserving the American buffalo?

A.Choice: Where can the American buffalo be found besides Yellowstone National Park?

Key.Rationale: This question would not lead to finding information about preserving the American buffalo.

B.Choice: When was the American buffalo selected as the state animal of Oklahoma?

Key.Rationale: This question would not lead to finding information about preserving the American buffalo.

C.Choice: Why were laws passed to make it unlawful to hunt the American buffalo?

Key.Rationale: This question would lead to finding information about preserving the American buffalo because it would help to find out about the laws that were enacted to help preserve the American buffalo.

D.Choice: What is the lifespan of the American buffalo?

Key.Rationale: This question would not lead to finding information about preserving the American buffalo.

SubTopics: Students will use apostrophes to show possession of singular and plural nouns and recognize and remove apostrophes used to form plurals.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:The two `text(trees)` leaves are turning brown.
What change, if any, should be made to `ultext(trees)` in the sentence?

A.Choice: tree's

Key.Rationale: In the sentence “trees” is a plural noun and needs an apostrophe added after the “s” to make it a plural possessive noun.

B.Choice: trees'

Key.Rationale: This shows that the leaves on multiple trees are turning brown.

C.Choice: treeses

Key.Rationale: This is the incorrect way to show the plural possessive of “trees.”

D.Choice: no change

Key.Rationale: “Trees” is the plural form of tree, but it does not show possession.

SubTopics: Students will capitalize familial relations, proper adjectives, conventions of letter writing, and the first letter of a quotation.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:My favorite relatives, uncle Juan and aunt Amalia, are coming for a visit.
Which words in the sentence should be capitalized?

A.Choice: uncle, aunt

Key.Rationale: The familial relationships “uncle” and “aunt” should be capitalized when used in front of their actual names.

B.Choice: favorite, relatives

Key.Rationale: “Favorite” is a common adjective, and “relatives” is a common noun.

C.Choice: are, coming

Key.Rationale: “Are” and “coming” are the verbs in this sentence.

D.Choice: a, visit

Key.Rationale: “A” is an article, and “visit” is a common noun.

SubTopics: Students will recognize parts of speech in sentences.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:I was surprised to see how much my cousin `ultext(grows)` since I last saw him.
What change, if any, should be made to `ultext(grows)` in the sentence?

A.Choice: growing

Key.Rationale: This is not a present perfect verb required by this sentence.

B.Choice: had grown

Key.Rationale: This is the correct past perfect verb required by this sentence.

C.Choice: will be growing

Key.Rationale: This is not a present perfect verb required by this sentence.

D.Choice: no change

Key.Rationale: This is not a present perfect verb required by this sentence.

SubTopics: Students will recognize parts of speech in sentences.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:I ran `ultext(slowly)` than my friend.
What change, if any, should be made to `ultext(slowly)` in the sentence?

A.Choice: slowlier

Key.Rationale: This is not the correct comparative form for the adverb “slowly.”

B.Choice: most slowly

Key.Rationale: This is the superlative form for the adverb “slowly,” not the comparative form.

C.Choice: more slowly

Key.Rationale: This is the correct comparative form for the adverb “slowly.”

D.Choice: no change

Key.Rationale: This is not the correct comparative form for the adverb “slowly.”

SubTopics: Students will compose simple and compound declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences, avoiding and correcting fragments.
Content: Read the sentences.
:ibox:The class picnic is next `text(Friday)`. I cannot go because of my brother's birthday party.
How can the sentences be rewritten as a compound sentence?

A.Choice: The class picnic is next `text(Friday)`, I cannot go because of my brother's birthday party.

Key.Rationale: This is an example of a comma splice, which uses a comma to separate `text(two)` independent clauses.

B.Choice: The class picnic is next `text(Friday)` I cannot go because of my brother's birthday party.

Key.Rationale: This is an example of a run-on sentence which does not use a period to separate `text(two)` independent clauses.

C.Choice: The class picnic is next `text(Friday)`. And I cannot go because of my brother's birthday party.

Key.Rationale: This is an example of a sentence fragment with the word “And” used to begin the second independent clause.

D.Choice: The class picnic is next `text(Friday)`, but I cannot go because of my brother's birthday party.

Key.Rationale: This sentence contains `text(two)` independent clauses connected by the coordinating conjunction but and a comma.

SubTopics: Students will recognize parts of speech in sentences.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:Bruce and Larry ride their bikes to school every day.
Which group of words in the sentence is a prepositional phrase?

A.Choice: Bruce and Larry

Key.Rationale: This is a compound noun.

B.Choice: ride their bikes

Key.Rationale: This is a verb phrase.

C.Choice: to school

Key.Rationale: This is a prepositional phrase using the preposition “to” followed by the noun “school.”

D.Choice: every day

Key.Rationale: This is an adverb phrase.

SubTopics: Students will recognize and correct errors in subject and verb agreement.
Content: Read the sentence.
:ibox:The entire team, including the sisters, run during practice.
What change, if any, should be made to the sentence?

A.Choice: The entire team, including the sisters, ran during practice.

Key.Rationale: “Team,” a collective noun, is the subject and takes a singular past tense verb in this sentence.

B.Choice: The entire team, including the sisters, runned during practice.

Key.Rationale: “Runned” is an incorrect past tense of the irregular verb “run.”

C.Choice: The entire team, including the sisters, running during practice.

Key.Rationale: The sentence requires a past tense verb; “running” is the present progressive tense.

D.Choice: no change

Key.Rationale: “Team,” a collective noun, is the subject and takes a singular past tense verb in this sentence.

SubTopics: Students will compare fiction, poetry, and nonfiction to distinguish various genres.
Content: A reader can tell the passage is nonfiction because

A.Choice: it is about real people and events.

Key.Rationale: A key feature of nonfiction texts is that they share information about people and places who really exist now or have existed in the past.

B.Choice: it has more than one character.

Key.Rationale: The number of characters is not a defining feature of nonfiction texts. Nonfiction and fiction texts can have multiple characters.

C.Choice: it is written in short sentences.

Key.Rationale: Short sentences can be in both fiction and nonfiction texts.

D.Choice: it takes place in the past.

Key.Rationale: Fiction and nonfiction texts can take place in the past.

SubTopics: Students will answer inferential questions using evidence from one or more texts to support answers.
Content: The reader can tell that Cracker Jack

A.Choice: is mainly eaten at sporting events.

Key.Rationale: There is nothing in the passage to suggest that Cracker Jack is mainly eating at sporting events. Paragraph `4` states that Cracker Jack was mentioned in a song about baseball, but there are no other references to sports in the passage.

B.Choice: has changed its coating many times.

Key.Rationale: Paragraphs `2` and `5` show that the molasses coating has only been changed `text(twice)`.

C.Choice: is the most common snack food today.

Key.Rationale: This information is not supported by the passage. Paragraph `8` indicates that it is still “part of the snack scene,” but no facts are provided to prove that it is the most common snack food.

D.Choice: has been enjoyed for many generations.

Key.Rationale: Paragraph `1` notes that Cracker Jack was first invented in `text(1893)`, and that it was “a big hit.” In `text(1908)`, the mention of Cracker Jack in the song “Take Me Out to the Ballgame” made the treat even more popular. Finally, paragraph `8` states that “Cracker Jack still remains part of the American snack scene today,” which supports the idea that it has been enjoyed for many generations.

SubTopics: Students will answer inferential questions using evidence from one or more texts to support answers.
Content: Why did the brothers `bbtext(most likely)` choose the name Cracker Jack?

A.Choice: They had a relative named Jack.

Key.Rationale: Paragraph `3` states that at the time Cracker Jack was invented, “cracker-jack” meant something very good. The name Cracker Jack was used to show that the treat itself was very good. In paragraph `6` it notes that the characters used to represent the treat were based on the inventor's grandson, not that they were named after him or any other relative.

B.Choice: They thought children would like it.

Key.Rationale: While it is probable that the term “cracker-jack” was a popular with children, it is not supported in the passage that children would like a snack named after a popular saying.

C.Choice: They knew it meant something that is very good.

Key.Rationale: “Cracker-jack” meant something very good, and the treat itself was very good. This information is supported by the details in paragraph `3`.

D.Choice: They thought Candied Popcorn and Peanuts was too long.

Key.Rationale: While “Candied Popcorn and Peanuts” is a long name, nothing in the passage suggests that anyone thought the name was too long. Rather, they wanted a name that conveyed how tasty the treat was.

SubTopics: Students will distinguish fact from opinion in an informational text and explain how reasons and facts support specific points.
Content: Which sentence from the passage contains an `bbtext(opinion)`?

A.Choice: It is made with popcorn, molasses, and peanuts, and it is delicious.

Key.Rationale: The first clause contains a fact-the ingredients can be verified. However, not all people will agree that the snack is delicious; it is not information that can be proven.

B.Choice: Cracker Jack made their box with red, white, and blue stripes.

Key.Rationale: This sentence is a fact. It can be proven by looking at boxes of Cracker Jack.

C.Choice: These characters were based on Frederick's grandson and his dog.

Key.Rationale: This sentence is a fact. It can be confirmed by looking at other sources

D.Choice: Once a prize is selected, it takes about a year for it to make it into a box.

Key.Rationale: This information can be verified by calling the company, so it is a fact.

SubTopics: Students will identify relationships among words, including synonyms, antonyms, analogies, homophones, and homographs.
Content: Which word is a synonym for `text(excited)` as used in paragraph `7`?

A.Choice: thrilled

Key.Rationale: Words that have the same or similar meanings are called “synonyms.” The words “excited” and “thrilled” both mean “extremely pleased.”

B.Choice: curious

Key.Rationale: “Curious” relates to one's attitude towards learning something new. Being excited is not the same as being curious.

C.Choice: grateful

Key.Rationale: “Grateful” means to be appreciative of “benefits received.” It has a different meaning than “excited.”

D.Choice: contented

Key.Rationale: “Contented” means to be satisfied with something. It suggests a calm manner. “Excited” suggests the opposite.

SubTopics: Students will compose simple and compound declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory sentences, avoiding and correcting fragments.
Content: Read these sentences from paragraph `2`.
:ibox:They called it Candied Popcorn and Peanuts. It was a big hit.
How could these sentences be rewritten as a compound sentence?

A.Choice: They called it Candied Popcorn and Peanuts, and it was a big hit.

Key.Rationale: A compound sentence consists of two independent clauses joined by a comma and a coordinating conjunction that shows the relationship between them.

B.Choice: They called it Candied Popcorn and Peanuts and it was a big hit.

Key.Rationale: Although a coordinating conjunction has been included, it is missing the comma preceding the coordinating conjunction.

C.Choice: They called it Candied Popcorn and Peanuts it was a big hit.

Key.Rationale: This is a run-on sentence. `text(Two)` independent clauses have been put together as a `text(single)` clause.

D.Choice: They called it Candied Popcorn and Peanuts, it was a big hit.

Key.Rationale: A comma has been used to join the `text(two)` clauses, but it is missing a coordinating conjunction.
